# Kind and Truth-Lo-
# ving Reader.

Recently, following the rumored report of my death, some idle mind presented me in the "Kingdom of the Dead" <note>A reference to the literary genre "Dialogues of the Dead," popular in the 18th century, where deceased historical figures engage in conversation.</note> as a General, alongside an actual military General. This style of writing is still the very latest fashion, even though it is already over fifteen hundred years old. Its first inventor was the incomparable <term>Lucian</term> <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – 180 AD), a Hellenistic satirist known for his wit and dialogues mocking philosophy and religion.</note>, as Saint <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347 – 407 AD), an important Early Church Father whose name means "golden-mouthed," referring to his legendary eloquence.</note> calls him. Chrysostom learned almost all of his <term>homiletics</term> <note>The art of preparing and delivering sermons.</note> and his art of preaching from this classical author. For this reason, it strikes me as a great wonder how most theologians—who are so very eager to emulate and even mimic Chrysostom—routinely refer to this teacher of "sacrosanct preaching" <note>original: sacrosanctæ Homiletices</note> as an arch-mocker of gods and men whenever they speak from the pulpit. The praise that Saint Chrysostom gives him deserves

<summary>The author responds to a satirical publication that used his rumored death to place him in a "Dialogue of the Dead," defending the genre's creator, Lucian, against theological critics.</summary>
<keywords>Lucian of Samosata, John Chrysostom, homiletics, satire, Kingdom of the Dead, preaching, 18th-century literature</keywords>

❧ (4) ❧

he deserves with great justice; for in his *Dialogues of the Heavens and the Underworld* <note>original: *Dialogis superum & inferum*</note>—that is, in the kingdoms of heaven and the dead—one finds, alongside great eloquence, an uncommon scholarship, many ancient histories, and a truly exceptional judgment. Indeed, those who so flippantly despise him reveal by doing so that they have no understanding at all. They really ought—even more so than their predecessor Saint Chrysostom and "Golden-Mouth" <note>A literal German translation of the name "Chrysostomus," derived from the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *stoma* (mouth). This refers back to the famous preacher mentioned on the previous page.</note>—to go to school under such a learned man. There, they could at least learn, to some extent, the highly famous "art of chatting"—otherwise known as the <term>Art of Preaching</term> <note>original: *Ars Homiletica*</note> and <term>Sacred Oratory</term> <note>original: *Oratoria sacra*</note>—even if they did not understand or perceive the rest of his work.

His other successor and <term>true disciple</term> <note>original: *genuinus Discipulus*</note> was also the excellent Erasmus of Rotterdam, who in his *Dialogues* or *Conversations* imitated him so successfully that one hardly knows which of the two should be given preference, except that the latter adapted the style to his own times and circumstances. Some believe these *Dialogues* of Erasmus of Rotterdam were written only for schoolboys; however, the profound Thomasius <note>Christian Thomasius (1655–1728), a famous German jurist and philosopher of the Enlightenment who advocated for education in the German language rather than Latin.</note> has judged quite rightly that they are the kind of things which one should keep until old age as a true core of theology and of all

From these three men <note>Lucian, Erasmus, and likely Christian Thomasius or the author himself.</note>, one should rightly make a cloverleaf <note>An idiomatic expression for a celebrated trio.</note>, because all three have combed through the priests' useless chatter, along with the confused nonsense of the bombastic <term>World-Wise</term> <note>original: *Welt-Weisen*; a term used for secular philosophers or sophists.</note>, far better than old Democritus <note>The ancient Greek "Laughing Philosopher" who mocked the follies of mankind.</note> ever did. If the current *Kingdom of the Dead* <note>A reference to "Dialogues of the Dead," a popular satirical genre where deceased figures discuss earthly follies; the author is likely critiquing a specific contemporary publication using this format.</note> were equal to its original invention, it would not vex me to fill a chapter within it myself; but because it has turned out so poorly and meagerly, I am hesitant whether I should weep over it out of compassion with Heraclitus <note>The "Weeping Philosopher," the traditional opposite of the laughing Democritus.</note> or laugh over it with Democritus; however, I shall stick with the latter. 

For instead of any formal refutation, I wish to demonstrate with this present writing that I am still very much alive, and that the joy of my enemies, as well as the sorrow of my friends over my feigned death, was something quite unnecessary. Anyone to whom my wonderful <note>In the 18th-century sense of "extraordinary" or "surprising."</note> fate and persecution is even slightly known can easily suspect that I must have intended more than once to withdraw myself entirely from this godless and honor-forgetting world. —less world, which to all honest and upright people is a well-known thing: that they are quite often driven and pushed—indeed, even hunted—into the wilderness, not so much by the Holy Spirit <note>original: *guten Geiste*</note>, but rather by "evil clergy" <note>The author is making a pointed pun on *Geist* (spirit) and *Geistliche* (clergymen/clergy).</note>. From this wilderness, they nevertheless sometimes return quite unexpectedly, to the great detriment of those persecutors, after much trial and temptation. This occurs even while those men are occupied with the "pious" thought that the Devil had long ago snatched the victim away and carried them off through the winds. Namely, it ultimately ends for all sincere followers and warriors of Jesus Christ as it is written: *Then the Devil left him*, along with all evil spirits and clergymen; *on the other hand, the angels came and served him.* <note>A reference to the ending of the Temptation of Christ in Matthew 4:11.</note>

Regardless of the fact that I have many times harbored such thoughts <note>i.e., thoughts of retreating into total isolation.</note>, I immediately let them pass again, as I know very well that according to the first divine decree <note>A reference to Genesis 2:18: "It is not good that the man should be alone."</note>, man was created not for solitude, but for the benefit of his fellow men and the whole of human society. Because of this, I saw clearly that I would have kept this hermit's life <term>Einsiedler-Leben</term> <note>A life of solitary religious retreat, often seen as a rejection of social responsibility.</note> just as little as Luther kept his monastic vows or his arrest at the Wartburg <note>The castle where Martin Luther lived in hiding as "Knight George" after being declared an outlaw; he eventually left his confinement to continue his work in the world.</note>. ...will, and as if—so to speak—the Spirit had not driven me into the wilderness. However, I am not willing to live here alone for myself, or to sit completely still, as I could very well do now; instead, I want to be a good **noisy spirit** <note>original: *Polter-Geist*. The author is playing on the word "poltergeist," a spirit that makes noise and causes trouble, suggesting he intends to be a disruptive force for the truth.</note>, like those people of whom it is said that they return or haunt, to see if I might perhaps cause some harm to the **cushion-clergy** <note>original: *Polster-Geistlichen*. This is a pun on "Poltergeist"; the author contrasts his own "noisy" activism with the "cushioned" or comfortable, lazy lives of the established ministers.</note> and awaken some people from this sweet sleep into which these **cushion-spirits** have so gently rocked them, and still rock and sing them to sleep. I wish to awaken them and make them alert, so that they might see as clearly as I and other honest people do, how these "spiritual Jews" <note>In the polemical style of the 17th century, the term "spiritual Jews" was a pejorative used by radical reformers to describe church leaders they believed were focused on legalism, ritual, and financial greed rather than the true Spirit.</note> deal with them through greed with fabricated words or barter them away, and also promise them the forgiveness of sins along with spiritual freedom and salvation, even though they themselves are slaves of corruption. These are men who day and night think of nothing else than how they might maintain their spiritual dominion and status of honor, along with all their prestige and income, through pleasant chatter on the **pulpit** <term>Cantzel</term> and in the **confessional** <term>Beichtstuhle</term>. They claim to have inherited this latter office from Matthias when he became an apostle, as a spiritual inheritance and another **patrimony of Peter** <note>original: *Patrimonium Petri*. This refers to the historical estates and temporal power of the Pope or the Church, here used sarcastically to mock the clergy's claim to authority and wealth.</note>. They seek to maintain this through certain ceremonies or spiritual processions, or to say it briefly and plainly in English: how they [deceive] the poor...

In it, an unknown friend requested that I should not pass him by upon my return to Germany; he intended not only to sufficiently reimburse my travel expenses, but he also lived in the hope that this visit would, in time, prove very useful and profitable to me. This letter, contrary to my habit, threw me into quite a state of unrest, especially since I had intended to instruct a good friend in **Copenhagen** in **chemistry** <note>original: "Chymie." The **theologian**, however, would neither stoop to **simony** <note>original: "Simonie"; the prohibited practice of buying or selling church offices or spiritual preferences.</note> nor conform to ancestral traditions; nevertheless, he was sought after by printers for his knowledge of languages. There, he had to serve as a **proofreader**, especially when secret writings were printed that would otherwise never have been permitted by the clergy. In this way, he earned his meager living, even though he might have had as much learning in his brain as half the ministry and more piety in his heart than the entire **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "Synedrium"; historically the supreme council of the Jews, used here to refer to the high ecclesiastical authorities or a formal religious assembly.</note>. 

The **jurist**, for his part, wished in his practice to follow only pure and unadulterated justice. For this reason, neither the judges cared to see him in court, nor did clients flock to him; consequently, despite all his righteousness, he would have surely starved had he not given music lessons and also taken on students for European languages.

<meta>This page continues the author's skeptical examination of how religious traditions are formed and maintained. It completes the sentence from the previous page regarding the claims made by various Christian sects.</meta>

For among a thousand people, there is hardly one who wishes to recognize and act upon the **truth** according to prescribed rules or laws. ### and of all evil.

[scholarsh]ip <meta>Continuing from the previous page, completing the word 'Gelehrsamkeit' (scholarship) or 'Freiheit' (freedom).</meta> have completely renounced the old Pythagorean **"he himself said it"** <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha). An ancient Greek phrase used to describe an uncritical appeal to a master’s authority rather than to reason or evidence.</note> or "He himself has said it." However, among **theologians**, this practice is taken to the absolute extreme. Yet, for that very reason, the least amount of truth is to be found among them. It is these very people who have for the longest time obstructed the progress of true **philosophy**, because they wished to simultaneously draw from their Grand Master **Aristotle**.

Specifically, anyone who demands that a parable or symbol must agree in every detail and circumstance with the thing being compared does not understand what a parable is; it usually looks only to certain circumstances or to the **point of comparison** <term>point of comparison: original "tertium comparationis," the specific quality that two different things have in common within a metaphor</term>, and pays no mind to the rest, because otherwise it would not be a parable, but the thing itself. The contribution that God makes to the actions of men gives him much to do; he wants neither too much nor too little of it. For this reason, those do not please him who would claim that the **preservation of the world** is a **constant new creation** <note>original: *beständige neue Schöpffung*; referring to the theological concept of *creatio continua*, the idea that God must actively uphold and "re-create" the universe at every moment to prevent it from vanishing</note>, because in such a case, all evil deeds could be deflected away from human beings and instead be burdened solely upon God. If one intended to honor God’s power too greatly, His justice and goodness would, in turn, be diminished by just as much. Therefore, there should be a **harmony** or agreement among all His attributes, such that what one cannot find in one attribute, one might seek in another. Whether one will actually find it there, however, is another question—one which Mr. von Leibniz has not settled, and yet he concluded his book with it, leaving the reader just as wise as they were before.

Now the question arises: What kind of law is this, which the soul must observe despite all its freedom? It is none other than the law of freedom, or the noble, indeed royal law of love, which Christ divided into two commandments: the love of God and the love of neighbor. Moses, however, presented it to the people of Israel in two tablets and ten commandments; yet in truth it is nothing other than the **natural law**, namely, that which sound reason teaches all people, if they only pay some degree of attention to it, and do not completely suppress this glorious gift of God through the prejudices of antiquity or the hearsay of their forefathers. 

Indeed, all of Moses' commandments are grounded in natural law, except for the single circumstance of the commandment regarding rest—namely, that it must necessarily be observed on the seventh day. Through this—as these people speak so grandiosely in their lack of understanding—the eternal justice of God might be satisfied. In this view, the justice of God is supposed to punish an innocent man in place of the guilty, which would actually be the height of injustice. One might well sing here from another song of Luther:

> He fell ever deeper into it, there was nothing good
> in his teaching; sin had possessed it.

Now, a fictional faith is supposed to grasp this merit of Christ with its hand, appropriating this foreign righteousness <term>fremde Gerechtigkeit</term> <note>original: "fremde Gerechtigkeit." A central Lutheran doctrine where a believer is not inherently righteous, but is "covered" by Christ's righteousness.</note> for itself, wrapping itself in it as if in a pure, flowery garment, and thus stepping before the judgment seat of God. Here, the blood of Christ is supposed to be of such great emphasis and power that—according to a dreadful poetic hyperbole <term>Hyperbole</term> <note>original: "Hyperbole." An intentional exaggeration for effect.</note> from an arch-Lutheran hymn—"even a tiny little drop can make the whole world clean," yes, even setting it free and clear from the devil's jaws. Since they have once brought such a flowery matter or symbol onto the stage <term>Theatrum</term> <note>original: "Theatrum." Referring to the "theater" or public arena of theological debate.</note>, they also play the comedy <term>Comödie</term> <note>original: "Comödie."</note> with nothing but such masked things.

# ...and of all evil.

...continues on and on, where the Law <term>Geseze</term> <note>original: "Geseze." Referring to the moral requirements and divine commands found in the Old Testament.</note> struggles with the Gospel <term>Evangelio</term> <note>original: "Evangelio." The Latin-derived term for the Good News or New Testament promise.</note>, and the Gospel with the Law; the former demands good works, and the latter wants only faith. This faith is then supposed to be an allegorical tree, which is afterwards expected to bring forth only fruits of faith instead of works—by no means as if these things should count for anything before GOD, but only out of gratitude for this great redemption through the fictional atonement-offering <term>Sühn-Opffer</term> <note>original: "erdichtete Sühn-Opffer." The author views the "penal substitution" model of the atonement—where Christ dies to satisfy God's legal anger—as a human invention or "fiction."</note>. And although they make this redemption and bloodshed—even just a single little drop of it—so great that it can cleanse the whole world, even making it free and clear of the devil’s gullet <note>original: "Rachen." Literally a throat or maw, often used to describe the "jaws of hell."</note>, yet the power of the wretched devil is still supposed to be so great that he will keep all nations and all people in his gullet for all eternity, if they did not possess the true Christian (perhaps Catholic or Lutheran) faith, or had not called upon and spoken the name of JESUS at their final end. 

O, that these people would go to the old Greek and Hebrew schools and learn what sacrifice, redemption, atonement, faith, name, works, justice, eternity, law, hell, life, death, and devil, etc. etc., actually mean! Then we would receive a completely different theology, which would not be filled with so many absurd, irrational, unfair, indeed abominable and truly blasphemous things. Through such things, no holy life nor good works—for which we were created by GOD—are promoted, but rather...

# On the Origin of Sin, etc.

...rather, all godliness <term>Gottseeligkeit</term> <note>original: "Gottseeligkeit." A state of piety or living in a way that is pleasing to God.</note> is hindered, and in its place, mere whims <note>original: "Grillen," meaning obsessive fancies or idle thoughts.</note> of idle and empty heads—which are just as bad as the old scholastic ones of the past—are brought into people's minds to their greatest harm and the obstruction of their future happiness. In particular, however, it looks quite foolish when these people set themselves to the Epistles of Paul and most of all to the Epistle to the Romans, masterfully translating them word-for-word just like schoolboys, and becoming so entangled in them that they know neither up nor down. This is especially true when they bring a completely pre-made <term>System</term> <note>original: "Systema," referring to an organized, rigid body of church doctrine.</note> into the text with them; they do not so much learn from Paul, but rather take this highly enlightened Paul to school, wanting to reform, turn, and twist him according to their lame tools. May **God** have mercy, and awaken more reasonable, zealous, and scripturally experienced people who might cleanse the <term>Augean Stables</term> <note>original: "Stabulum Augiæ." A reference to the Greek myth of Hercules cleaning the stables of King Augeas, which had not been cleaned in thirty years; here, it refers to clearing out centuries of corrupt or "filthy" theological traditions.</note> of this supposed theology in a paternal manner from all the ancient manure and filth. They should instead introduce a **Divinity** <term>GOttes-Gelahrtheit</term> <note>original: "GOttes-Gelahrtheit." An archaic term for theology or the study of God's word.</note> worked out solely according to the Scriptures and according to sound <term>Hermeneutics</term> <note>original: "Hermenevtica." The branch of knowledge that deals with interpretation, especially of the Bible.</note>. This is so that we might finally obtain a reasonable worship <term>Gottesdienst</term> <note>original: "Gottesdienst." Literally "God-service," referring to both formal church services and the internal devotion of the believer.</note> for the honor of the all-wise **God** and for the improvement and salvation of reasonable people. To this end, I for my part—as long as I still live—shall never cease to apply all my remaining strength.

# On the Origin of Sin, etc.

...but rather all piety is hindered, and in its place nothing but the whims of idle and empty heads—which are just as wicked as the old scholastic <term>scholasticism: a medieval method of learning that emphasized dialectical reasoning and was often criticized by later reformers for being overly technical and philosophical</term> ones once were—are brought into people's minds to their greatest detriment and the hindrance of their future blessedness. 

Especially, however, it appears quite foolish when these people set upon the Epistles of Paul, and most of all the Epistle to the Romans, masterfully translating them word-for-word just like schoolboys, and becoming so entangled in them that they know neither which way is out nor which way is in. This is especially true when they bring a completely finished *system* <note>original: "Systema"</note> into the text with them; they do not so much learn from Paul, but rather take this highly enlightened Paul to school, wanting to reform, turn, and twist him according to their own lame ideas. 

May **God** have mercy, and awaken more sensible, zealous, and scripturally experienced people who might clean the *Augean Stables* <note>original: "Stabulum Augiæ"; in Greek mythology, Hercules was tasked with cleaning stables that had not been mucked out for thirty years, representing a near-impossible task of purification</note> of this so-called theology in a fatherly manner, purging it of all its ancient dung and filth. Instead, they should introduce a **Godly**-Learning <note>theology</note> worked out solely according to the Scriptures and sound *hermeneutics* <note>original: "Hermenevtica"; the study of the principles of interpretation, especially of the Bible</note>, so that we might finally receive a sensible worship for the honor of the all-wise **God** and for the improvement and salvation of sensible people. To this end, for my part, as long as I still live, I shall never cease to apply all my remaining strengths.

### End of the first part.

<summary>The author concludes the first part of his work with a passionate plea for a return to scriptural theology, arguing that modern theologians "twist" the words of the Apostle Paul to fit their own rigid systems. He calls for a cleansing of theological tradition, likening the task to the mythological cleaning of the Augean Stables.</summary>
